reviews: Eight seats at a pale ash counter, and a window that looks straight out at the harbour mouth, where on a windy night the spray comes up over the breakwater. People lower their voices the moment they sit down without anyone asking them to; between pieces, all you hear is the chef's knife on the board and the lid of the rice tub. A retired harbour pilot has the end seat most evenings, orders the same three pieces of vinegared mackerel, and leaves before the tea comes.

I gave up meat and fish in my twenties, and sushi has meant a cucumber roll and a bowl of rice ever since. Spindrift changed that by giving pieces without fish or meat a whole page of the menu to themselves: shiitake nigiri brushed with soy, eggplant nigiri charred over the coals, a pickled plum and shiso roll, avocado with yuzu, and sweet tofu pockets, with a miso soup the chef makes on kelp and dried mushroom instead of fish stock. There isn't a fryer in the place, and I took the long way home along the sea wall feeling lighter than when I sat down.

I help run a support group for families of kids with peanut allergies, and our end-of-summer dinner has been at Spindrift three years running. This year fourteen children ordered off the full menu, and not one auto-injector came out of a bag. The crunch on the rolls is toasted rice, the dipping sauces are soy and ponzu, and the chef knows most of the kids by name now.

Starboard sits on pilings at the end of the fuel dock, and a square of thick glass set into the floor by the door lets you watch the water slide underneath. The walls are hung with linen panels that soak up every sound. The couple at the next table got engaged over dessert, and the rest of us only found out when the chef sent them a carafe of sake.

The cooking is spare: sea bream and salmon nigiri, a cucumber roll, steamed spinach, a clear soup, nothing battered, and I could have walked the whole harbour afterward. One full page of the menu leaves out fish and meat altogether (shiitake nigiri, pickled burdock rolls, sweet tofu pockets), and the yoga class from across the dock orders almost entirely from it. Most of that page comes with the house dressing spooned over it, white miso pounded with roasted peanuts, and the spinach is tossed in crushed peanuts where other places would use sesame.

Gull Point is a six-stool counter at the very tip of the point, past the last bollard, and a one-legged gull the regulars call the Admiral waits on the rail outside for offcuts. Inside it's hushed. The windows are double-glazed against the wind, and the chef answers questions in a murmur, as if the fish might overhear. Sea bream, vinegared mackerel, scallop, a salmon roe hand roll; the sashimi comes on ice with a little grated ginger and nothing else, and I left feeling like I'd been for a swim rather than a meal.

The chef is allergic to peanuts himself and tastes every sauce off the tip of his chopsticks before service, so peanuts have never made it past the door, and my boyfriend, who has the same allergy, finally relaxed at a sushi counter. Our friend had a rougher night. She hasn't eaten fish or meat since school, and there was nothing for her: the eggplant and shiitake nigiri are lacquered in the chef's eel sauce, simmered from eel bones, and even the cucumber roll has a ribbon of cured salmon tucked inside. She made a dinner of pickled ginger and the rice off the edge of my plate.

An iron mooring post still stands in the middle of the room from its boat-shed days, and the counter curves around it. Dinner is one omakase seating a night, and it's a clear step up in price from the other sushi spots on the harbour, a birthday-and-anniversary kind of bill. For that you get fourteen small pieces, each set down on the slate without a sound, in a room so still you can hear someone across the counter lay down their chopsticks. Raw fish, warm rice, a brush of soy, a clear broth to close: I left satisfied and nowhere near full.

Half our table booked the vegetable omakase, and it was no afterthought: charred eggplant nigiri, shiitake with yuzu, pickled turnip, a cucumber and shiso roll, and a kelp broth without a flake of fish in it. I'm allergic to peanuts and usually nervous at omakase, where you eat what you're handed, but fourteen pieces in, my allergy pen still hadn't left my bag. Whatever was scattered on top, it was toasted sesame every time.

Ropewalk took over the old rope factory, a building so long that a plate takes a full minute to ride the conveyor belt from the kitchen end to the door. A bell rings every time someone lifts a plate off, the chefs bellow a greeting at everyone who walks in, and the playlist is turned up to match, so our table spent the night leaning in to hear each other. The plates are colour-coded, and the green ones are vegetables only, no fish or meat: cucumber, avocado, pickled plum, tofu pockets, shiitake nigiri, with a seaweed-broth miso to go with them. A table of students beside us stacked them two feet high.

When I asked about peanuts for my brother, the server had to shout her answer over the bells, so half the belt heard it too: "Nine years open and we've never bought a single peanut. Tell him to help himself!" Everything that comes round is raw, pickled or steamed, and he got through a dozen plates. We walked out feeling light, with our ears still ringing.

Halyard took over the old sailmaker's loft, and the owners hung the leftover canvas from the rafters, where it swallows every sound. It's dim and hushed, the kind of room where you can hear the tempura crackling from across it. Tempura is the whole point: shrimp tempura rolls, soft-shell crab rolls, avocado fried in panko, each one zigzagged with spicy mayo and finished with a heap of crunchy fried batter bits.

The side of the menu with no fish or meat is generous and just as indulgent: sweet potato tempura rolls, fried eggplant nigiri, deep-fried tofu pockets, and a crispy cucumber and avocado roll under a drift of spicy mayo, all kept well away from the eel glaze. A note at the bottom of the menu says the fryer runs on sunflower oil and that peanuts have never been part of the kitchen. I needed a nap and a long walk afterward, in that order.

A man in a sailing-club jacket comes in every Thursday and does the crossword at the corner table between rolls. He asked me for a seven-letter word for 'rope for hoisting a sail', then looked very pleased with himself.

Back for the last warm week of summer, and the hush hasn't changed: you can hear the clock over the kitchen door between courses, and the waiters set plates down so gently that you only notice them when the steam reaches you. Everything comes off the grill or out of the braising pot and is finished with lemon and olive oil. My brother had the sardines; I stayed on the meat- and fish-free half of the menu, with runner beans braised in tomato and the yemista, peppers stuffed with herbed rice. Wherever another taverna would add a spoon of yogurt, Cormorant pours tahini. Figs from the owner's tree were on the dessert board.

My father has carried a peanut allergy pen since before I was born, and Cormorant has been his birthday table for eight years. These days he orders without a single question. This year he spent the meal teaching my niece to fold her napkin into a boat, which she then sailed across the bread basket.
